props.title: Death Promise

sections.content: **Death Promise** (1977) stands as a fascinating artifact of 1970s exploitation cinema, emerging from New York City's grindhouse scene when martial arts films were exploding in popularity. Following **Enter the Dragon** (1973) and the surge of Bruce Lee-inspired movies, Death Promise merged kung fu action with gritty urban vigilante themes that dominated films like Death Wish (1974). The film's plot about tenement residents fighting back against corrupt landlords reflected real NYC housing issues, making it a unique hybrid of martial arts and social commentary.

sections.content: Death Promise director Charles Bonet only made this one feature film, but it captures a distinct moment when independent filmmakers were crafting ultra-low-budget responses to both mainstream martial arts imports and successful vigilante films. Like **Dolemite** (1975) and **Black Belt Jones** (1974), it represents the creative ways American filmmakers incorporated kung fu into stories reflecting urban American experiences.

The film's fight choreography, while rough by today's standards, shows clear influence from Shaw Brothers classics like Five Fingers of Death (1972) and **The 36th Chamber of Shaolin** (1978). Lead actor Charles Bonet trained in actual martial arts, giving the fights an authentic if unpolished quality rarely seen in contemporary low-budget productions. sections.content: Death Promise's blend of martial arts and social issues wasn't unique to the 1970s. Films like **Berry Gordy's The Last Dragon** (1985) and **China Girl** (1987) continued exploring urban martial arts themes through the 1980s. The film's focus on housing corruption and class struggle predates similar themes in **The Super** (1991) and **Vampire in Brooklyn** (1995), though those later films took more comedic approaches.
